title: Tunneling amplifies chirality-induced spin selectivity and explains its current-direction invariance
authors: Fedor Baranov, Virginia Gali, Gal Lemut, Maxim Breitkreiz
abstract: We propose a minimal model for chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) in dc transport through insulating chiral molecules, based on quantum tunneling and interaction-induced spin splitting. As a concrete realization of the latter, we consider a weak Zeeman interaction of the particle spin with the current-induced magnetic field, recently shown to occur in helical molecules. We show that quantum tunneling, combined with dissipation, amplifies the effect, so that even such a small spin-dependent perturbation can yield spin polarizations on the order of 100\% across a wide range of applied bias voltages. Furthermore, our tunneling scenario naturally reproduces the characteristic CISS symmetry of the current-voltage dependence -- namely, the invariance of the spin-polarization sign under reversal of the current direction -- while fully respecting Onsager's reciprocity relations.
summary: The paper proposes a theoretical model explaining Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) in molecular junctions by combining quantum tunneling theory with dissipation. It shows that even weak, current-dependent spin perturbations can lead to near-perfect spin polarization. This mechanism successfully explains the observed symmetry of CISS regarding current reversal while remaining consistent with fundamental transport laws.
main_problem: The study aims to elucidate the mechanism behind Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) in dc transport through insulating chiral molecules, particularly explaining how large spin polarization can arise while respecting fundamental symmetries.
main_result: Quantum tunneling combined with dissipation is shown to amplify small spin-dependent perturbations, yielding high spin polarizations ($\sim 100\%$) and naturally reproducing the characteristic current-direction invariance of CISS.
method: The analysis employs theoretical modeling using a 1D scattering approach, incorporating the WKB approximation for tunneling probabilities in the presence of a weak Zeeman interaction derived from the applied current.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as quantum tunneling through an insulating chiral molecule placed between two leads. The physics is governed by spin-dependent molecular orbital energies ($V_\sigma$) perturbed by a current-induced magnetic field, and dissipation is included via an external resistor ($R$).
key_observables: Spin Polarization (SP), relative transmission difference ($T_{	ext{split}}$), and the dependence of these quantities on applied bias voltage ($V_b$) and molecular length ($L$).
important_parameters: The characteristic mean free path ($\ell_\alpha$), the magnitude of the Zeeman coupling ($\alpha(I)$), and the resistance $R$ (which extends the measurable voltage range).
main_assumptions: The model assumes that single-particle descriptions are insufficient due to Kramers' degeneracy, necessitating the inclusion of dissipation. The analysis relies on the WKB approximation for tunneling.
figures_summary: Figures compare current ($I_\sigma$) vs bias voltage ($V_b$) curves with and without an added resistor ($R$), demonstrating that $R$ extends the voltage range where high SP is maintained. Another figure confirms the scaling of SP with system length $L$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the model by first establishing the necessity of dissipation to overcome single-particle limitations, then deriving the tunneling probabilities using WKB, and finally demonstrating how the resulting current-voltage characteristics naturally exhibit the required symmetry (current-direction invariance).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses spin transport phenomena in nanoscale molecular junctions, which is a key area bridging condensed matter physics with quantum chemistry and AMO concepts like spin-orbit coupling effects on tunneling.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of spin-dependent tunnel- ing across a helical molecule with current-induced magnetic field B. For positive voltage bias (top right), the energy level of tunneling particles (filled circles) is closer to LUMO. Due to current-induced Zeeman splitting of LUMO, the barrier is lower for spin up (blue), which leads to a larger current for spin up than for spin down (see I-V curve below the figure). For negative voltage bias (top left), the charge current and thus the Zeeman splitting are opposite and the tunneling par- ticles are closer to HOMO. The barrier is again lower for spin up. Spintronics.note: The paper directly addresses spin polarization and spin-dependent transport in molecular junctions, which is a core topic within spintronics, even though the mechanism (tunneling/dissipation) differs from cavity QED.
